title: Zig tutorial: types, slices, error unions, comptime and allocators — cv.cm
description: Learn Zig basics: install and run Hello world, use const and var, arrays and slices, optionals, error unions with try and catch, defer, comptime and allocators.
answer: Zig is a general-purpose systems programming language and toolchain meant as a modern alternative to C. It has no hidden control flow, no garbage collector and no hidden memory allocations: you pass an allocator explicitly, handle errors with error unions and `try`, and clean up with `defer`. Compile-time code execution (`comptime`) replaces macros and generics. Run a file with `zig run hello.zig`. Zig is still before version 1.0, so details of the language and standard library change between releases.

sections.h: What Zig is and who uses it
body: Zig was created by Andrew Kelley and is developed by the non-profit Zig Software Foundation. It targets the same work as C: operating system components, embedded firmware, game engines, databases and fast command-line tools. The Zig compiler can also compile C and C++ code (`zig cc`) and cross-compile to many targets, so some projects use it only as a C toolchain.
Well-known projects written in Zig include the Bun JavaScript runtime, the TigerBeetle financial database and the Ghostty terminal emulator.

body.note: Zig is pre-1.0. Syntax and especially the standard library change between 0.x releases, and tutorials written for an older version may not compile. This page keeps to basics that have been stable for several releases; always read the documentation for the exact version you installed (`zig version`).

sections.h: Install Zig and run Hello, world
body: Download a prebuilt archive for your system from ziglang.org/download, unpack it and add the folder to your PATH, or install Zig with your system package manager. There is no separate installer or runtime.

body.code:
zig run hello.zig         # compile and run
# Hello, world!
zig build-exe hello.zig   # produce an executable named hello
zig init                  # create a project with build.zig

body: `std.debug.print` writes to standard error and is the simplest way to print in every recent version. The second argument is a tuple of values for the format placeholders; `.{}` is an empty tuple. The API for writing to standard output has changed between releases, so check your version's standard library docs for it.

`const` declares a value that never changes and `var` declares a mutable variable. The compiler is strict: an unused local variable is an error, and a `var` that is never modified is also an error, so use `const` by default.

body: Format placeholders say how to print: `{d}` for numbers, `{s}` for strings, `{c}` for a single byte as a character, `{any}` for debugging any value.
`if`, `switch`, `while` and `for` can all be used as expressions. `switch` must cover every possible value, so you usually add an `else` branch.
`[_]u8{ ... }` lets the compiler count the array length. `for (items, 0..)` loops over the items and a counter at the same time; the values between pipes are called captures.

Functions declare the types of parameters and the return type. Arguments are immutable inside the function. Generic code is written with `comptime` parameters: a type is a value that exists at compile time, so a function can take a type as an argument.

The compiler creates a separate version of `max` for each type it is called with. The same mechanism is used to build generic data structures in the standard library: a function that takes a type and returns a new struct type.

sections.h: Error handling with error unions, try and defer
body: Errors are values. A return type `!u32` means "a `u32` or an error". `try expr` returns the error to the caller if there is one; `catch` handles it on the spot. Errors cannot be ignored silently.
`defer` runs a statement when the current block exits, and `errdefer` runs it only when the block exits with an error. They keep cleanup code next to the code that acquired the resource.

Zig has no garbage collector and no global hidden allocator. Any function that needs heap memory takes an `std.mem.Allocator` parameter, so the caller decides where memory comes from (the page allocator, an arena, a fixed buffer, or a debugging allocator that detects leaks).

`|*slot|` captures a pointer to each element so the loop can write to it, and `slot.*` dereferences the pointer. In Debug and ReleaseSafe builds, integer overflow and out-of-bounds indexing stop the program with a clear panic instead of causing undefined behavior.

sections.h: A small complete program: average of numbers
body: The program splits a string on spaces, parses each piece with `try`, stores the numbers in heap memory freed by `defer`, and returns an optional average that is `null` for an empty list.

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: leaving a local variable unused or declaring a `var` that is never changed (both are compile errors); using `{}` without a specifier for strings (use `{s}`); forgetting that string literals are byte arrays, not Unicode characters; mixing integer types without an explicit cast such as `@intCast`; and copying code from a tutorial written for an older Zig version.

faq.a: Some companies use Zig in production, but the language is pre-1.0, so you should expect breaking changes when you upgrade the compiler and plan time for them.

faq.q: Is Zig a replacement for C or for Rust?
faq.a: Zig is closest to C: manual memory management with better safety checks, error handling and compile-time code. Rust guarantees memory safety through its ownership system and borrow checker, which Zig does not have.
Yes. Zig can import C header files and call C functions directly, and the Zig compiler can build C and C++ source files, which makes mixing the languages straightforward.

faq.q: What does comptime mean in Zig?
faq.a: `comptime` marks code or parameters that are evaluated while compiling. Zig uses it for generics, constant tables and compile-time checks instead of a separate macro language.
